newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait may tax company profits by 2000 - minister.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait may tax company profits by 2000 - minister.

text.p: Kuwait could impose taxes on local firms by the year 2000 as part of its efforts to eliminate its budget deficit, Planning Minister Ali al-Zmei'a said on Wednesday.
"Tax imposition, if any, would be on the profit of institutions and firms," Zmei'a, talking about the government agenda until the year 2000, told a news conference.
Such a step needs the approval of parliament, he noted without giving details.
But a "tax on individuals' income is a matter that does not exist nor is being studied," he said.
Kuwaitis enjoy state services that are either free or at subsidised rates.
"There is no (such thing as) constant welfare...the welfare process is passing (throught) a dangerous and critical stage," he said. "The door is open for all financial policies."

The government has said it plans to eliminate the state budget deficit by the year 2000. It projects a deficit of 1.2 billion dinars ($4.0 billion) in the 1996/97 year (July-June). Higher than expected oil prices have helped Kuwait reduce to 653 million dinars a projected 1.32 billion deficit in 1995/96.
Zmei'a said inflation in 1995/96 was less than two percent.
The deficit has been eroding Kuwait's foreign reserves, an oversees nest-egg designed to support it when its oil runs out.
The reserves, once estimated at about $100 billion, fell to about $35 billion chiefly due to the costs of the 1991 Gulf War, which ended Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait.

"The deficit issue is not only economic and social...events prove that it has a security dimension," said Zmei'a. Economists say Kuwait needs to boost its reserves to withstand possible threat to its security.
"Despite the relative improvement in the budget deficit in the past years, the danger of this deficit growth still exists," he said. "We cannot control oil prices."
"It is important to continue increasing non-oil revenue and rationalising spending," he said without elaboration.
Government officials have said they were considering increasing charges on state services and cuting state spending and subsidies as means to reduce the deficit.

Zmei'a told Reuters the government, required by law to provide a job for every Kuwaiti seeking one, wants to freeze the number of civil servants at current levels. State wages account for over a third of the state revenue.
"The philosophy is to freeze (state jobs) at the current volume," said Zmei'a. "The government is not required to provide public sector jobs (namely)," he added.

Zmei'a said the state wants to raise to six percent the Kuwaiti workforce share of private sector jobs from a current 2.1 percent by the year 2000. About one million workers work at the private sector.
"A public job is not (anymore) a tool for wealth distribution as it was at a certain stage. It is a tool to produce wealth," he said.
Most working Kuwaiti nationals are employed by the state. The private sector depends almost totally on cheap foreign workers from Arab and Asian states.
Officials say job cuts for Kuwaitis are unthinkable.
